messages.subject: Re: BioGeoBEARS error
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Jun 3, 2017 at 6:38 AM, Itanna Oliveira Fernandes <itanna.f...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear Nick,
>
> I am trying to run the BioGeoBEARS and in my very first try I got the following error:
> Error in matrix(data = NA, nrow = ntips, ncol = nareas) :
>   invalid 'nrow' value (too large or NA)
> I was running RStudio and my input were a newick tree (from FBD model) and txt doc with the species from the FBD model and their respective zoogeographic areas.
> The matrix has 234 taxa (4.258bp) and some of those have more than one individual of the same species (i.e. Anochetus mayri I88, Anochetus mayri I01, ...).
> I am totally new using R, as well, in systematic. So, could you please help me to figure this out?
> Best regards,
>
> Itanna
>
>
> Itanna Oliveira Fernandes
> Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas da Amazônia - INPA
> Coordenação em Biodiversidade CBio/Entomologia
> Av: André Araújo, 2936. Petrópolis.
> Manaus - AM. Brasil, 69067-375.
>
> http://fauna.jbrj.gov.br/fauna/faunadobrasil/2617
> http://lattes.cnpq.br/5126000463150115
>

Hi -- several issues here:

1a. Your geog file:

=============
T N F I A P
Euponera_rovana_I130_0.0 0 0 1 1 1 0
Simopelta_jeckylli_I18_0.0 1 0 0 0 0 0
Brachyponera_sennarensis_I132_0.0 0 0 1 1 0 0
Cryptopone_butteli_I41_0.0 0 0 0 1 1 0
Dinoponera_quadriceps_I23_0.0 1 0 0 0 0 0
Neoponera_villosa_I16_0.0 1 1 0 0 0 0
[...]
=============

1b. Correct geog file:
=============
233 6 (T N F I A P) Euponera_rovana_I130_0.0 001110 Simopelta_jeckylli_I18_0.0 100000 Brachyponera_sennarensis_I132_0.0 001100 Cryptopone_butteli_I41_0.0 000110 Dinoponera_quadriceps_I23_0.0 100000 Neoponera_villosa_I16_0.0 110000
[...]
=============

See example files, and advice on text editors, here:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#files

2. Your newick file has apostrophe characters in it (').  This means they don't match the species names in the geog file. I deleted them.  The example script says:

#######################################################
# Phylogeny file
# Notes:
# 1. Must be binary/bifurcating: no polytomies
# 2. No negative branchlengths (e.g. BEAST MCC consensus trees sometimes have negative branchlengths)

3. The newick file has 3 negative branchlengths. I fixed this with impose_min_brlen().  This is addressed here:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#short_branches

http://phylo.wikidot.com/testing-for-fixing-common-tree-file-problems-in-biogeobears
(search on "impose_min_brlen")

Sending fixed files off-list, they run fine after the fixes...

Cheers, Nick

messages.body_plain:
Dear Nick,

I am back again. This time I am working a relatively large tree with 218 terminals. After running the DEC and DEC+J model, I had a graph which showed area F as the ancestral area for several nodes, I then decided to get the probabilities of states/ranges at each node and I realized it completely did not match the results from the graph.
For example

NODE   TABLE   GRAPH (probabilities of states/ranges)

248           F                  AB

250           F                  AB

260           F                  AB

292           F                  AB

297           F                  AB

298           F                  AB

350           F                  AB

352           F                  B, D, AD

359           C                 B

363           C                 B

376          C                  A/AB/B

389      B/AC                B/AB

393           E                 D

400           E                  C

……………………………….etc

I have attached the tree file with node numbers, range probabilities file, and the graphical result.

Also, I have attached my tree file, geodata, and R.script in case you have time to run and tell me what is happening.

My maximum number of areas is 4.

Thanks in advance

MC

messages.subject: Two jump dispersals from one node?
messages.subject_clean: Two jump dispersals from one node?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nick,

I am working on a biogeographical analysis using the DEC+J model and find some equivocal reconstructions. Specifically, there is a lineage with ancestral area (A) that splits in two clades that each are unique to a particular area (B and C). The equivocal scenarios are either A->B->C or A->C->B. This makes sense as it is impossible to estimate which of the two is better.

However, I can imagine a third scenario that is missing from the results: namely that the lineage dispersed from A to B AND C (i.e. jump dispersals to two different areas, see image below).

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-9mUPtskFFfs/WUWwLk-65YI/AAAAAAAAF6o/JuwLd7FwI9cuqRt1BHJyRNoquSwqmZT8wCLcBGAs/s1600/Scenario_3.png>
Because this scenario is never reconstructed, I suspect that this is a limitation of the analysis (indeed, there is no such scenario in the BioGeoBEARS supermodel graphic <http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic>).

My question is why such a scenario is not reconstructed and if there is a workaround?

Thanks!

Robin van Velzen

3. Run the script "script_v2.R" EXACTLY

Everything in the script should work then.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Two jump dispersals from one node?
messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] Two jump dispersals from one node?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Robin!  Thanks for the question!

It is true that scenario is not programmed in the standard models,
therefore it will not be reconstructed (but see below*).

It wouldn't be that hard to add the scenario as an option, but the
biological justification seems weak. I totally believe that an ancestral
population could produce jump dispersals to two regions basically
simultaneously ("basically simultaneously", i.e. close together as measured
over millions of years).  However -- why would that simultaneously make the
ancestor go extinct?

Even if one figured out a reason for that, these models (DEC etc)
effectively assume zero lineage extinction, i.e. a Yule or pure-birth
process, i.e. the observed tree is treated as the complete tree.  Adding
lineage extinction requires an BiSSE-like model or something similarly
elaborate (and computationally very slow for large numbers of states --
BiSSE has only 2 states).  This assumption sucks, but it is very common in
many phylogenetic comparative methods (or it is effectively assumed, if
extinction is estimated but comes out near zero, which is common).

Hope this helps!
Cheers, Nick

PS: If you *did* see such a scenario in an ancestral-states plot under the
standard models, it would be a case of this:

The plot of most-probable states is not the same thing as the best joint
history
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_joint

...and related to my usual mantra...

Ancestral range estimation, not ancestral area reconstruction
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#ace_not_arr

PPS: And, when interpreting biogeographical ancestral ranges plots,
remember that neither traditional parsimony nor traditional continuous-time
likelihood models are good interpretive frameworks for the likelihood
models in biogeography:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#intro

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick,

Many thanks for the quick response and explanations. This confirms what we suspected.

I was referring to the stochastic mappings but we did not see such a scenario in the ancestral states plot either - just the two equivocal scenarios. But I think a two-jump dispersal is at least theoretically plausible in our case (if one can assume one 'jump' dispersal with immediate extinction in the ancestral area, why not two dispersals with extinction immediate after the second dispersal). But I totally see how this would be difficult to model realistically without taking into account lineage extinction (or lack of sampling).

I will write something short along those lines in our discussion.

Thanks again & cheers!

Robin

Hi, leaving for Evolution 2017 in a bit, brief comment:

On Mon, Jun 19, 2017 at 5:28 PM, Robin van Velzen <robinv...@gmail.com> wrote:

But I think a two-jump dispersal is at least theoretically plausible in our case (if one can assume one 'jump' dispersal with immediate extinction in the ancestral area,

A one-jump dispersal event definitely does not assume immediate extinction in the ancestral area!  The ancestral population continues, and is represented by the other lineage at the lineage-splitting event.  I suppose you could call this "pseudo-extinction" of the "ancestral species" when one species splits into two, but clearly that's not real extinction.

E.g. ancestor lineage lives in B;

Figure 1:

BBBBBBBBBB

Jump dispersal happens, founds a new population in A:

Figure 2:

BBBBBBBBBBBBB
                             |
                             A

...both continue:

Figure 3:

BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB
                             |
                             AAAAAAAAAAAAAA

We show this in typical phylogenies like this, basically because it is annoying/difficult to re-do the tree drawing software (and would be especially difficult when probabilities are not 100% etc.):

Figure 4:

                            BBBBBBBBBBBBBB
                             |
BBBBBBBBBBBBB
                             |
                             AAAAAAAAAAAAAA

But, Figure 4 and Figure 3 are showing you identical events.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Yes - of course. Thanks for the correction and clarification! So the issue of not finding two jump dispersals is strictly due to lineage extinction (or lack of sampling):

Figure 5 Two jump dispersals:

                                                             CCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC
                                                             |
BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB*extinct/unsampled*
                             |
                             AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA

Have a great time at Evolution!

Robin

On Mon, Jun 19, 2017 at 9:43 AM Nick Matzke <mat...@nimbios.org> wrote:

> Hi, leaving for Evolution 2017 in a bit, brief comment:
>
>
> On Mon, Jun 19, 2017 at 5:28 PM, Robin van Velzen <robinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Nick,
> >
> > Many thanks for the quick response and explanations. This confirms what we suspected.
> >
> > I was referring to the stochastic mappings but we did not see such a scenario in the ancestral states plot either - just the two equivocal scenarios. But I think a two-jump dispersal is at least theoretically plausible in our case (if one can assume one 'jump' dispersal with immediate extinction in the ancestral area,
>
> A one-jump dispersal event definitely does not assume immediate extinction in the ancestral area!  The ancestral population continues, and is represented by the other lineage at the lineage-splitting event.  I suppose you could call this "pseudo-extinction" of the "ancestral species" when one species splits into two, but clearly that's not real extinction.
>
> E.g. ancestor lineage lives in B;
>
> Figure 1:
>
> BBBBBBBBBB
>
> Jump dispersal happens, founds a new population in A:
>
> Figure 2:
>
> BBBBBBBBBBBBB
>                              |
>                              A
>
> ...both continue:
>
>
> Figure 3:
>
> BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB
>                              |
>                              AAAAAAAAAAAAAA
>
> We show this in typical phylogenies like this, basically because it is annoying/difficult to re-do the tree drawing software (and would be especially difficult when probabilities are not 100% etc.):
>
>
> Figure 4:
>
>                             BBBBBBBBBBBBBB
>                              |
> BBBBBBBBBBBBB
>                              |
>                              AAAAAAAAAAAAAA
>
>
> But, Figure 4 and Figure 3 are showing you identical events.
>
> Cheers!
> Nick
>
>
>
>
> > why not two dispersals with extinction immediate after the second dispersal). But I totally see how this would be difficult to model realistically without taking into account lineage extinction (or lack of sampling).
> >
> > I will write something short along those lines in our discussion.
> >
> > Thanks again & cheers!
> >
> > Robin
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Monday, June 19, 2017 at 6:53:35 AM UTC+2, Nick Matzke wrote:
> > > Hi Robin!  Thanks for the question!
> > >
> > > It is true that scenario is not programmed in the standard models,
> > > therefore it will not be reconstructed (but see below*).
> > >
> > > It wouldn't be that hard to add the scenario as an option, but the
> > > biological justification seems weak. I totally believe that an ancestral
> > > population could produce jump dispersals to two regions basically
> > > simultaneously ("basically simultaneously", i.e. close together as measured
> > > over millions of years).  However -- why would that simultaneously make the
> > > ancestor go extinct?
> > >
> > > Even if one figured out a reason for that, these models (DEC etc)
> > > effectively assume zero lineage extinction, i.e. a Yule or pure-birth
> > > process, i.e. the observed tree is treated as the complete tree.  Adding
> > > lineage extinction requires an BiSSE-like model or something similarly
> > > elaborate (and computationally very slow for large numbers of states --
> > > BiSSE has only 2 states).  This assumption sucks, but it is very common in
> > > many phylogenetic comparative methods (or it is effectively assumed, if
> > > extinction is estimated but comes out near zero, which is common).
> > >
> > > Hope this helps!
> > > Cheers, Nick
> > >
> > > PS: If you *did* see such a scenario in an ancestral-states plot under the
> > > standard models, it would be a case of this:
> > >
> > > The plot of most-probable states is not the same thing as the best joint
> > > history
> > > http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_joint
> > >
> > > ...and related to my usual mantra...
> > >
> > > Ancestral range estimation, not ancestral area reconstruction
> > > http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#ace_not_arr
> > >
> > > PPS: And, when interpreting biogeographical ancestral ranges plots,
> > > remember that neither traditional parsimony nor traditional continuous-time
> > > likelihood models are good interpretive frameworks for the likelihood
> > > models in biogeography:
> > >
> > > http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#intro
> > >
> > > Cheers!
> > > Nick
> > >
> > > On Sun, Jun 18, 2017 at 8:49 AM, Robin van Velzen <robinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Dear Nick,
> > > >
> > > > I am working on a biogeographical analysis using the DEC+J model and find some equivocal reconstructions. Specifically, there is a lineage with ancestral area (A) that splits in two clades that each are unique to a particular area (B and C). The equivocal scenarios are either A->B->C or A->C->B. This makes sense as it is impossible to estimate which of the two is better.
> > > >
> > > > However, I can imagine a third scenario that is missing from the results: namely that the lineage dispersed from A to B AND C (i.e. jump dispersals to two different areas, see image below).
> > > >
> > > >  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-9mUPtskFFfs/WUWwLk-65YI/AAAAAAAAF6o/JuwLd7FwI9cuqRt1BHJyRNoquSwqmZT8wCLcBGAs/s1600/Scenario_3.png>
> > > > Because this scenario is never reconstructed, I suspect that this is a limitation of the analysis (indeed, there is no such scenario in the BioGeoBEARS supermodel graphic <http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic>).
> > > >
> > > > My question is why such a scenario is not reconstructed and if there is a workaround?
> > > >
> > > > Thanks!
> > > >
> > > > Robin van Velzen
> > > >
